title: LiteLLM supply chain compromise
description: On October 21, 2026, the LiteLLM Python proxy library version 1.107.0 was compromised in a supply chain attack. The malicious release was available on PyPI and official Docker images for approximately two hours. Attackers used stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from three engineers to deploy a malicious fork via a private release workflow. The payload included a credential stealer targeting cloud, developer, AI-tool, browser, and LiteLLM proxy credentials, as well as a second-stage remote access trojan backdoor. The malware executes automatically whenever Python starts by placing files in the site-packages directory. This is the second known supply chain compromise of LiteLLM in 2026, unrelated to the previous incident linked to TeamPCP activity.
aiSummary: The LiteLLM supply chain compromise involved attackers leveraging stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from three engineers to push a malicious release of LiteLLM version 1.107.0. This release was distributed via PyPI and official Docker images for about two hours before removal. The malicious payload installed a credential stealer targeting various credentials including cloud, developer, AI-tool, browser, and LiteLLM proxy credentials. Additionally, it deployed a remote access trojan backdoor that executes automatically on Python startup through files dropped in the site-packages directory. This incident represents a repeated supply chain attack on LiteLLM in 2026, with no confirmed link to the earlier compromise attributed to TeamPCP. No CVE or patch information is available at this time.
aiImpact: The compromise allowed attackers to steal sensitive credentials across multiple domains (cloud, developer tools, AI tools, browsers, and LiteLLM proxies) and maintain persistent remote access via a trojan backdoor. This could lead to unauthorized access to critical systems and data. The malicious release was live for a short window (about two hours), limiting exposure but still posing significant risk to users who downloaded the compromised version during that time. There is no evidence of active exploitation beyond the supply chain compromise itself.
